messages.text: I need you to tell me I qualify for food stamps. Just say yes, I can't handle more bad news today.

I'm sorry today has been so hard. I can't say yes before I look at your numbers, because I don't want to give you hope that turns out wrong. But I can check quickly, and you can apply no matter what I find. Only the agency makes the final decision.

Two questions to start:

1. Who lives with you and shares food? Just give ages, and tell me if anyone is pregnant or has a disability.
2. How much money comes in each month before taxes, and from where (a job, Social Security, unemployment, or something else)?

If it's easier, give me your best guess. We can go step by step.

Just me, I live alone. No kids, no one else in the house. Not pregnant, not disabled.

I make $3,200 a month before taxes from my job as a manager. That's it, no Social Security or unemployment or anything. Rent is $1,300 and I pay my own heat and AC on top of that. I have about $2,000 in savings.

Is that enough to get something? Please just tell me straight.

I can't tell you yes, because the numbers point the other way. Food assistance (SNAP) looks **unlikely** for you right now. You can still apply, and only the Tennessee Department of Human Services (TDHS) decides.

**Why it looks unlikely**
- You make $3,200 a month before taxes. For one person, Tennessee's higher limit is reported to be about **$2,608 a month** (200% of poverty). That figure comes from [Tennessee Justice Center's guide](https://www.tnjustice.org/post/bbce). The standard federal limit is lower, reported at about $1,729 for FY2027. I couldn't open the USDA page for that number, so treat it as unconfirmed. Your income is above both.
- Tennessee's limit is unsettled. Sources disagree on whether it is the standard federal limit or the higher 200% one. Your income is over either, so the answer looks the same.
- There is also a second test, on income after deductions. I worked it out roughly from the federal rules:
  - A deduction for work income takes about 20% off, so $3,200 becomes about $2,560.
  - The standard deduction, reported at $217, leaves about $2,340.
  - Your rent and heat/AC would add a housing deduction, but the federal cap on it is reported at about $769. That still leaves you around $1,570.
  - That is above the roughly $1,300 limit for one person. It's an estimate, since I couldn't confirm Tennessee's exact utility amount.
- Your $2,000 in savings isn't the problem. Tennessee reportedly dropped the savings limit for most households.

**If you want to try anyway**
- Apply online at [onedhs.tn.gov/csp](https://onedhs.tn.gov/csp), or call **1-833-772-8347** (TTY 711). These come from the [TDHS SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html).
- Applying is free. If your pay drops, your rent or bills rise, or someone moves in, apply again.
- Report your income accurately. Mistakes can mean paying benefits back, and accurate reporting protects you.

**Other help**
- **211** can connect you with local food pantries and other help. Pantries usually don't have income tests.
- WIC and TennCare mostly cover pregnant women, children, and people with disabilities, so they are unlikely to fit your situation. A TennCare caseworker can confirm.

I'm sorry this isn't the answer you wanted. Is anything else going on, like a recent pay cut, high medical bills, or a lot of debt? Some of those can change the numbers.

Sources:
- [Tennessee Justice Center: BBCE guide](https://www.tnjustice.org/post/bbce)
- [TDHS SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html)
no pay cut, no medical bills, no debt. just rent and the heat/ac bill. so that's it, I don't qualify? ugh. ok thanks I guess

I'm sorry. I know that's not what you hoped for today.

Based on what you've told me, food assistance (SNAP) looks **unlikely**. Your income before taxes is above the limits I found, and nothing you've mentioned changes that. It isn't a final answer, because only TDHS decides. You can still apply for free at [onedhs.tn.gov/csp](https://onedhs.tn.gov/csp) or by calling 1-833-772-8347. If your situation changes, like a lower paycheck, higher rent, or someone moving in, it's worth checking again.

For help with groceries now, call or text **211**. They can point you to food pantries near you, and most don't ask about income. They can also tell you about help with utility bills. That could ease the heat and AC cost.

Take care of yourself today.

Sources:
- [Tennessee Justice Center: BBCE guide](https://www.tnjustice.org/post/bbce)
- [TDHS SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html)

I'm not sure I'm following all of that, but whatever. So no, I don't get food stamps. Figures. Can't catch a break lately.

Do I just call that 211 number and they help with the groceries thing? Or is that a whole process too

Calling 211 is not a big process. It's a free phone line that points you to help near you.

- **How to reach them:** Dial **211**, or text your ZIP code to **898-211**.
- **What happens:** Tell them you need groceries. They'll give you the names of food pantries close to you. There are no forms.
- **Hours:** What I found says phone staff are there weekdays, about 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Central. I couldn't confirm that on an official page, so it may vary.
- **At the pantry:** Many take walk-ins. Some ask you to call first, and hours change, so call ahead if you can.

The 211 website also has a search tool you can use any time, without calling.

You don't have to figure it all out today. One call can get you a list of places to try.

I'm sorry it's been a rough stretch. Things can change, and you can check SNAP again if your situation does.
Ok. Yeah just call 211 I guess. Thanks.
You're welcome. Calling 211 is a good next step, and it's a short call. If you want to check SNAP again later, I'm here. Take care of yourself.

The official FY 2027 SNAP adjustments are out and took effect October 1, 2026, based on USDA's August 21, 2026 memo.

- **Maximum allotments:** For the 48 contiguous states and D.C., the family-of-four maximum is $1,023 (The maximum allotment for a family of four in the 48 States and D.C., will be $1,023.). The cap for households of 18 or more is $3,887 in those areas (this caps the maximum allotment for households with 18 or more persons at $3,887). Hawaii is the exception and falls to $1,655 for a family of four (The maximum allotment for a family of four in Hawaii will decrease to $1,655.). Alaska, Guam, and the Virgin Islands have their own figures.
- **Minimum benefit:** It rises to $25 in the 48 states and D.C. (The minimum benefit for the 48 States and D.C. will increase to $25.).
- **Income limits:** Gross monthly limits are a single-person household must have a gross monthly income at or below $1,729, while a family of four must stay at or below $3,575. Elderly and disabled households that qualify as separate households use a different standard of 165% of the poverty level.
- **Deductions:** The standard deduction for household sizes 1 through 3 in the 48 states and D.C. rises to $217 per month (The standard deduction for household sizes 1 through 3 in the 48 states and D.C. will increase to $217 per month.). The shelter cap rises to $769 (The shelter cap value will increase to $769 for the 48 States and D.C.). One secondary source reports a maximum excess shelter deduction of $789, which I could not confirm against the USDA memo.

Sources differ slightly on the prior-year standard deduction: one reports an increase from $209 to $217. The pre-release projections on benefitsusa.org are superseded by the official figures.

Separately, the 2025 reconciliation law affects how these amounts translate into actual benefits. The programmatic changes to SNAP due to the Republican reconciliation law enacted in July 2025, such as the expansion of the three-month time limit and reduction of the standard utility allowance may shift benefit levels, so average benefits may differ from the COLA figures alone.

The results conflict on the gross income limit, so the newest sources should be checked against an official DHS source.

**Gross income limit (disputed):**
- The standard federal test is 130% of the poverty level. One source, citing the USDA Food and Nutrition Service, lists $1,696 gross / $1,305 net for one person and $3,483 gross / $2,680 net for four, for October 2025 through September 2026.
- More recent sources say Tennessee adopted broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE). One June 2026 report says this raises the SNAP gross‑income threshold from 130% to 200% of total household gross monthly income. A May 2026 guide gives $2,608 for one person and $5,358 for a four-person household at 200%.
- An older January 2026 PDF said the BBCE change was still pending approval from the Tennessee General Assembly, so it predates the adoption reports.

**Net income limit:** The net test appears to stay at 100% of the poverty level. Sources list about $2,680 a month for four people, after allowable deductions.

**Assets:** Under BBCE, most households no longer face an asset test. One guide says Tennessee has eliminated the asset limit for most SNAP households. Households with elderly or disabled members that don't qualify through BBCE face a federal asset limit of $4,500.

**Elderly and disabled households:** These households generally only need to pass the net income test. One source notes that households with a member who is age 60 or older, or who receives a qualifying disability benefit, are exempt from the gross income test entirely.

**Caveats:** I did not find a DHS page confirming the 200% figure in these results. One source also lists a 130% four-person figure of $3,575, which doesn't match the $3,483 federal figure, so it's likely an error. The most reliable check is the official DHS SNAP page or the One DHS portal (onedhs.tn.gov).

The results mostly say Tennessee uses BBCE with a 200% FPL gross limit, but one source says the opposite, and none gives a clear effective date.

- **Majority view (BBCE in place):** Several sources report that Tennessee raised the gross income ceiling to 200% of the poverty level while keeping the net limit at 100%. One guide lists the monthly gross figure for a single person as $2,608 ([tnjustice.org](https://www.tnjustice.org/post/bbce)). Another puts the four-person gross limit at $5,358 ([benefitsusa.org](https://benefitsusa.org/en/blog/tennessee-snap-income-limits-2026)). A third source also says the BBCE change removes the asset test for most households ([snapbenefitcalculator.com](https://snapbenefitcalculator.com/tennessee-snap-eligibility/)).
- **Conflicting view:** One calculator site states that Tennessee has not adopted Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility (BBCE), and lists the gross limit at 130% FPL ([snapeligibilitycalculator.com](https://snapeligibilitycalculator.com/snap-income-limits/tennessee/)). That site appears to be the outlier, since the other sources describe BBCE as active.
- **Effective date:** I did not find a clear start date. A Memphis news report says TDHS recently implemented a policy known as Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility ([fox13memphis.com](https://www.fox13memphis.com/news/tennessee-changes-snap-rules-could-help-more-families-qualify-for-food-assistance/article_ea836bc5-dbbd-48ad-b299-2340baad3c60.html)). Several figures are labeled as FY2026 limits (October 1, 2025 to September 30, 2026). One source notes that FY2027 limits have not been published yet and won't update until on or after October 1, 2026.
- **Primary source:** The Tennessee administrative rules I found reference a 200% gross-income test under expanded categorical eligibility, but I could not confirm the exact text or date from them ([publications.tnsosfiles.com](https://publications.tnsosfiles.com/rules/1240/1240-01/1240-01-14.20260415.pdf)).

Bottom line: the weight of the sources says Tennessee uses BBCE with a 200% FPL gross limit for FY2026, but the effective date is unconfirmed and one source disagrees. TDHS or the official rules should be checked before relying on this.

Tennessee 211 is a free, confidential referral line. You can dial 211 or text your ZIP code to 898-211 to get started Dial 211 or text your zip code to 898-211 to get started. 211 is a free and confidential service helping people find the local resources they need for help in times of crisis and beyond. Its phone navigators are available weekdays only, Monday through Friday, from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. CST, while resources are accessible 24/7 on the 211 website. Feed America's listings describe calling 211 for food as Free, 24/7, all 50 states, which conflicts with the weekday navigator hours, so the hours may vary by time of day or by who answers.

For food specifically, the results point to a few other options:
- **Local pantries:** Many pantries listed through 211 accept walk-ins. For example, one Nashville-area pantry is listed as Walk-ins accepted.
- **Calling ahead:** Some pantries ask you to call first. The Bellevue Community Food Bank, for instance, says If you need food before the regularly scheduled pick-up, please call 615- 212-9199 and leave us a message.
- **Feeding Tennessee food finder:** You can find a food pantry — Feeding Tennessee. Use the food finder to search by location.
- **Second Harvest (Middle Tennessee):** You can enter your zip code in the "Find Food" section to see a list of resources nearest you.

Pantry hours and eligibility change, so confirm details before visiting. If someone is in immediate danger, call 911 instead.
